['1.  
Welcome possible Day,  
Welcome, double welcome, Candlemas;  
None may match you;  
You, whose name carries great weight.  

2.  
Thus cried the dry Gang,  
Always thirsty, always eager;  
Fed on Hare loins;  
Sharply toothed, like a saw.  

3.  
Jan, startled by this sound;  
I bet he would rather have seen a Ghost:  
He was well used at home;  
Where it is always Lady Feast day.  

4.  
It was also on the second of this month,  
That his Claertje had her birthday;  
Whom he courteously served, dear Reader,  
Don’t think otherwise, it was well arranged.  

5.  
That he had a young son,  
When he was Claertje’s Lord and Man;  
The child was as beautiful as a statue,  
And alabaster was what covered him.  

6.  
Don’t praise it, ask the Peat farmer,  
Who said to Cunis, “Oh Man,  
I wish that were in your marrow,  
What? that poor Akkerman.”  

7.  
Words fill no sack here,  
And even less empty stomachs.  
Oh, my legs are so weak;  
That they can hardly carry the empty body.  

8.  
I become so ill; where is the Table?  
Hold me a quart in front of my nose,  
Set wine here; and there a waffle:  
It’s good, even if it’s entre deux.  

9.  
Blooming hearts, it is quiet here;  
Besides, we are no talkers:  
When a person wants to say something,  
Suddenly it’s, well, a lot of chatter!  

10.  
I choke on my food;  
Give another a turn:  
Silence there; suddenly what morsels!  
Wonder that his stomach does not tear.  

11.  
But whatever everyone thinks or says,  
I still laugh just as much about it:  
And for some impudence,  
I drink one glass more for it.  

12.  
Don’t you think that best, Uncle Peter?  
I have the weariness of the lonely hermit;  
No, I find it here a bit better:  
He may go home if he wants.  

13.  
I am tired of porridge and beans,  
And the disgust rises from flatfish;  
No, it goes much lively here,  
That people drink until they are full.  

14.  
I bring you, Candlemas, says one;  
I thank you, Candlemas, says the other:  
Would a stranger not think,  
That people were brothers with each other?  

15.  
All of the same name,  
Birds of the same feathers;  
Et Cantare pares t’ zaem,  
Et parati respondere?  

16.  
If you want to go chat by the Neighborhood,  
Go out with new shoes;  
All the rubbish from the streets  
Jan has brought into his house.  

17.  
No, it’s not fished from him,  
And he might well wish for the crowd;  
By my reckoning, it is so,  
Truly a Lazymart of people.', 'What one hears and sees today,  
The very best Fools;  
Who late at night, across the street;  
With girls making faces,  
This great joy, now fully delights,  
They know no work;  
No craftsman leaves the jug,  
To strengthen the thirsty heart.  
I will now here, with much pleasure,  
Let you once hear,  
What a craftsman, mostly can,  
At this time delight,  
One who swears, another who rages,  
With curses swearing fiercely,  
And on this path I quickly tell you  
That his noble masters.  
The printers and the typesetters,  
Who are famous everywhere;  
One at the press, and the other with the letters,  
Each mastering the art of the desk,  
But they know well enough,  
Also to empty their glass once in a while,  
Because the sweet fair delights.  
Everyone’s heart is joyful.  
See the barber’s boys raging once,  
With their fair coins at hand.  
They go home and swing merrily;  
It’s as if they are grown men,  
One sees their turns,  
With girls and nags.  
Is that dirty? Is that not?  
Although they do curl hair,  
Because there are also good ones.  
Masons and carpenters,  
Do not forbid themselves this.  
Being joyful once,  
And going to strum the strings,  
All to have a glass to drink  
At this joyful fair delight.  
And the bookbinders,  
Do not like swearing at all.  
But they are excellent,  
Lovers of cleaning their throats,  
When they empty a goblet.  
That is what they are known for.  
Many grinders of diamonds are found,  
Who are coopers and like to dress up.  
With many a young girl,  
With whom they once, properly,  
Go to carouse.  
And play very gallantly as great gentlemen.  
Here also,  
Many wigmakers;  
Who weave and prepare hair,  
They also know well enough,  
To nicely clear their throat.  
With the noble grape’s juice,  
Tapped from the bagass barrel,  
They drink it full and drunk;  
The shoemakers’ journeymen shine in all,  
To run quickly from one to another hole.  
To drink under one, swing near the peat  
Like the wet one wants, the barrel is very mean.  
The smith finds the fire too hot,  
Therefore he does not want to work,  
And says I am already clothed,  
I must strengthen my heart,  
Even with a fresh Rhenish wine,  
At the fair one must be merry.  
Who could blame that,  
To stop working now.  
The bell founder by his pot,  
Does not want to be foolish now.  
But watches where he pleases,  
In the playhouse or in the stuff,  
Because it is considered mere nonsense,  
Those who now do not join,\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0bis.  
Joy persists in this fair time.  
The sculptor lets his claws,  
Stand still for a while,  
To empty the glass,  
He thinks properly  
Now I have done my work.  
The painter also goes to entertain himself,  
As summer now comes to an end,  
One glass two three would at least not harm him,  
And each buys one to drink sometimes;  
With full glasses, like great masters.  
Are these not fools, when it goes like this?  
The cooper knows no block,  
The dry shearer no cloth.  
They let it all stop,  
The hat maker dances,  
This is also imprinted.  
One sees it all bustling,  
The weaver knows no reels.  
It all wants to be merry,  
They drink beer and wine bravely.  
It all runs into hundreds,  
Everyone speaks quite amazed.  
The fair is clear,  
It comes but once a year.  
Stonecutters with heaps,  
And sawyers also with one.  
Also buy a glass.  
Because that is common,  
The cheerfulness rises,  
To the highest peak,  
There is no fear with it.  
Even if everything was gone.  
The tailor must also dance,  
Even if he has no shirt at the hole.  
So with raging and with swearing,  
Often drunk or half drunk,  
Like boatmen’s journeymen strong,  
Often do this as well.  
Although there is no coin or cross in the house,  
Nor food to feed themselves.  
Those enjoyments are just foolishness,  
For those who live here in joy.  
But that running around,  
And that fooling,  
My day gives no benefit at all.', "How long that journey also takes;
It is now the fourth year;
How sadly fearful that time falls upon me!
I took an East Indies sailor,
A sea dog, fresh, healthy, and strong,
Greatly loved by the ship's crew,
Also by his Officers, as I notice:
A man like a child.

Thoroughly learned in ship work,
A truly experienced man:
Who neither fights, nor swears, nor drinks, nor curses,
Who can speak fiercely
When it is necessary, and otherwise not.
Oh, if I could see him again,
There would be an end to my sorrow;
How welcome he was!
Look, whether I say it or stay silent
I am very uneasy,
Because I get no word or answer...
Who knows on which coast
The ship has come to grief! Perhaps
It perished with man and mouse...
Oh Bram, shall I never see you again?
Won't you come home to your wife!

Who knows where he travels and wanders!
Whether he suffers from hunger!
And is sick and sighing, even dying.
I may have already lost him.
It is already far beyond the year
Since I last saw his spirit;
I sat with the child, and he stood there,
By bright clear day.
He looked quite well,
So handsome, so well made:
It is certain that this means something good;
He looked earnestly at the child.
There he stood, in his long trousers,
No six feet from me;
I saw very clearly the silk cloth
That I had given him as a gift:

Naturally, tied around his neck.
How immensely happy I was!
I had long hoped for this sight.
I thought, he is thinking of me.
My Bram was never a frivolous fellow,
Says everyone who knows him.
He has a valuable intellect;
Oh, he is such a good man!
I got this child when he was still
Less than eight weeks at sea.
He was well-made in body and limb,
It went well with him.
People suspected I served for Min
Regarding that:
But I had no intention of that,
I declined the Lady.

I give my child what God gave me
For the little blood.
I also promised it to my husband, and he
Left me on this.
Come to mother, sweet Jan;
Oh, if your daddy were here!
If he saw you, I know the man
Would cry with joy.
Yes, if you only knew, my dear Bram,
How day and night,
I cared for our little lamb;
How I fulfilled my duty!
He left my sight not once;
I earned my bread with the needle.
I feared gossip more
Than the pale death.

But why do I torment myself so
And worry, and sigh, and cry.
The man probably has it well;
I can, after little time,
See him again, healthy and fresh.
That would be a joy!
‘Then it’s a new fair again’:
So says my neighbor Styn.
And see, she already knows this of old;
That I can well guess:
Sailors always have good wives,
That is all we do.
They visit us so cheerfully,
They don’t look stern or angry:
Hear, it doesn’t grieve me that for myself
I chose a handsome sailor girl.

What is the noise in the street?
It is already flying towards Westdyk...
It’s as if guns are firing too!
I’ll go and look as well;
So I get the right information;
Come with me, mother, Jan.
There lies the ship; look, Jantje, there.
Oh Lord, there stands my husband."]
